extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent applicants, and IP practitioners (especially in AMS jurisdictions and PCT practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing inventive step (non-obviousness), definition/scope of the person skilled in the art (PSIA), combining prior art, secondary considerations, industrial applicability, and amendment practice under PCT/AMS examination practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solution approach
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-step approach: (i) determine the closest prior art; (ii) establish the objective technical problem to be solved; (iii) consider whether the claimed invention, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, would have been obvious to the PSIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in several AMS (e.g., Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Viet Nam). Emphasises identifying the closest prior art and an objective technical problem; contrasts with Windsurfing which focuses on the inventive concept rather than the single closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing/Pozzoli test
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step test: (i) identify the claimed inventive concept; (ii) assume the mantle of the PSIA and impute the common general knowledge at the relevant date; (iii) identify differences between the cited prior art and the alleged invention; (iv) viewed without knowledge of the invention, decide whether those differences would have been obvious to the PSIA or require invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not require identification of a single 'closest prior art' but rather the most relevant prior art. Restated in Pozzoli as: (1)(a) identify the notional PSIA (b) identify common general knowledge; (2) identify inventive concept or construe it; (3) identify differences; (4) decide obviousness absent knowledge of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: PSIA is a hypothetical person with common general knowledge in the relevant art and the ability to use ordinary technical means for R&D; has ordinary or average skill (not extraordinary), can exercise ordinary creativity in selecting materials, optimising ranges and replacing elements with equivalents, and can comprehend technical matters of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PSIA is not the inventor. Exact level of skill must be defined per case. Standard sets a floor for inventive step and excludes extraordinary skill. May represent a group (e.g., research/production team) in complex technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited capability of PSIA (no inventive capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: PSIA is proficient in relevant field details but does not have inventive capabilities; combinations or mosaics of prior art are permitted only if they can be put together by an unimaginative person with no inventive capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reminds examiners that the PSIA cannot be taken to predict future developments; ordinary creativity allowed but not inventive insight. Defines limits on permissible combinations of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of common general knowledge of PSIA
rubrics_metrics.description: PSIA is presumed to have access to all publicly available prior art information, able to comprehend all technical matters in the relevant art, capable of applying conventional experimental methods available before the date, and aware of what was common general and field-specific knowledge at the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common general knowledge may be shown by textbooks, handbooks, monographs, encyclopedias, and reference works. Some scientific facts so self-evident may be taken as present within the PSIA's intellectual arsenal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art (permissibility conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining or mosaicking teachings of two or more prior art references is permissible only where such combination would be obvious to the PSIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners usually consider: (i) whether nature and content of the prior arts make it likely the PSIA would combine them; (ii) whether the prior arts come from similar or neighbouring technical fields or are reasonably pertinent to the particular problem. Motivation need not match the applicant's; single-document combinations allowed if a reasonable basis exists to associate parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining with common general knowledge and textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is normally obvious to combine a well-known textbook or standard dictionary with other prior art; it may also be obvious to combine two documents when one contains a clear reference to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case of combination with common general knowledge. Prior art may suggest the claimed invention for a different purpose and still render it obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection inventions (selected sub-sets/sub-ranges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection inventions that represent selected sub-sets or sub-ranges can involve an inventive step if the selection is connected to a particular technical effect and there are no indications that would lead the PSIA to make that selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the same technical effect occurs in the broader known range, an unexpected degree of effect within the selected range may justify inventive step. Consider whether the PSIA would have made the selection in expectation of improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (factors to support inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to be taken into account as secondary considerations: (i) whether the claimed invention fulfils a long-felt need; (ii) whether it overcomes a scientific prejudice; (iii) whether others previously attempted and failed to achieve the invention; (iv) whether it involves an unexpected result; (v) whether it has particular commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are persuasive pointers towards non-obviousness. Detailed national practices vary and are listed in CSR Chapter 11, section 11.1.6.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a scientific prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention solves a technical problem that workers in the art have long tried to solve, fulfils a long-felt need, or overcomes a scientific prejudice, the examiner should be hesitant to raise a negative inventive-step determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat overcoming scientific prejudice as an important technical factor supporting inventive step; see PCT ISPE GL guidance for particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior art leads the PSIA away from the procedure proposed by the claimed invention (i.e., teaches away), this generally indicates an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies particularly when the PSIA would not consider experiments to determine alternatives to the known way of overcoming a technical obstacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected technical progress or advance
rubrics_metrics.description: An unexpected technical effect may indicate inventive step, but it must derive from the claimed subject-matter (characterising features), not from additional description-only features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected effect must be described in precise terms; vague statements (e.g., 'unexpectedly good properties') cannot support inventive step. The product/process need not be objectively 'better', only that the effect would not have been expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeable disadvantageous modification (negative indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention results from a foreseeable disadvantageous modification of the prior art that the skilled person could predict and assess, and that disadvantage is not accompanied by an unexpected technical advantage, then the claimed invention does not involve an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere foreseeable worsening, an arbitrary non-functional modification, or an arbitrary choice from many possible solutions does not support inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success as secondary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial or economic success can be indicative of inventive step but not by itself decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success must derive from the technical features of the claimed invention (not from marketing) and be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention. Immediate commercial success when coupled with evidence of long-felt need is relevant if tied to technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of the inventor's stated problem when assessing inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention should be disclosed so that the technical problem(s) it deals with can be appreciated and the solution understood; only necessary details should be included, and an explicit problem-and-solution presentation is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doubt exists about required details, the examiner should not require excision. Refer to PCT ISPE GL Chapter 4 on disclosure of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and disclosure of advantageous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantageous effects are among the secondary considerations; applicants should state any advantageous effects they consider the invention to have relative to the prior art, but must not disparage prior products/processes or mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some AMS require explicit statement of advantageous effects; statements must not give a false impression about prior art and should avoid ambiguous presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later-submitted data (admissibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Later-submitted data will be considered by the examiner only if submitted in response to an office action and must not go beyond the scope of the application as originally filed or introduce new teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission depends on the individual case; data must be supported by original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality and substantiation of advantageous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged advantageous effects must be supported by analysis linking structural features of the invention to theoretical explanation or experiential data; paper or hypothetical examples may be insufficient in presence of contrary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require specific, precise description and, where possible, empirical support rather than vague assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations supporting non-existence of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention arises from a foreseeable disadvantageous modification, arbitrary non-functional modification, or arbitrary choice from many solutions, and lacks unexpected advantage, these support a finding of lack of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See EPO Guidelines Part G for examples; national practices vary but follow similar reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims dependency and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim is regarded as limited by all features of the claim on which it depends; if the independent claim has a positive inventive-step finding, dependent claims should normally be positive; if independent claim lacks inventive step, inventive-step assessment should be made for each dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should use PCT ISPE GL examples as guides but avoid forcing a case into an inapplicable example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Industrial Applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial applicability (susceptibility of industrial application) requires that an invention can be made or used in some kind of industry; 'industry' is broad (includes agriculture, handicraft) and covers physical activities of technical character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not override patentable subject-matter exclusions (e.g., surgical methods). Inoperative inventions (contrary to well-established laws of nature) do not comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability test (three conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three required conditions: (1) the application must indicate how the invention is capable of exploitation in industry (intended function, special purpose or specific use); (2) the application must disclose the invention sufficiently clear and complete for a PSIA to carry it out (or rely on public sources available before priority date); (3) it must be actually possible for a PSIA, when carrying out any claim, to realise the indicated special purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is carried out as of the priority date. Examples and appendices in PCT ISPE GL Chapter 14 elaborate each requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special purpose (industrial applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The special purpose should be readily apparent from the claim subject-matter or from the nature of the invention; certain inventions (e.g., novel chemical compounds) require indication of specific use in the application to meet this requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no specific use is indicated for compounds/processes, the first requirement may not be complied with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and complete disclosure for industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The application is sufficient if it, together with information available from public sources before priority date, enables a PSIA to carry out the claimed subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both from viewpoint of carrying out the invention and from viewpoint of finding required information in prior art. Example: specifying a heat expansion ratio may suffice even if the material is not named, provided the material is known in prior art; if neither known nor manufacturable from disclosure, requirement fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of realising the special purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification of compliance with the third industrial applicability requirement assesses technical correctness: implementing the invention as claimed must result in an embodiment capable of being used for the indicated special purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perpetuum mobile is an example that fails even if disclosure is clear. Technical errors that prevent usability for the special purpose also cause failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date at which industrial applicability requirements must be met
rubrics_metrics.description: All three industrial applicability requirements must be met as of the priority date of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information incorporated into the application after the priority date cannot be used to establish industrial applicability as of priority (would be added matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for appealing rejection for lack of industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant should be allowed to file a response with explanation, data, or evidence addressing examiner objections; admission of the response depends on the case but is usually possible if supported by the original disclosure; appeal to an administrative body or court is available if rejection is upheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may consider submitted data if support exists in the original disclosure; procedural specifics vary by AMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments must not add subject-matter (formal and substantial allowability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments (pre- and post-grant) must not add technical subject-matter not disclosed in the application as originally filed and must not introduce other deficiencies (lack of clarity, lack of unity). Correction of obvious mistakes is generally allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices on what constitutes added matter are consistent across AMS. Post-grant amendment less common; full disclosure of optional features and combinations at filing is vital to preserve amendment flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant amendment procedures and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-grant amendments can be filed voluntarily before filing the search and examination request, or when responding to the examiner's written opinion/objection; applicants must request amendments in the prescribed manner within prescribed periods and submit required documents and fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant fails to comply with requirements, the Registrar may refuse the request. Pre-grant changes must be considered for search and examination unless filed after the search and relate to unsearched subject matter (jurisdictional variations exist).
